title: What the world calls @
hook: In Italy the @ is a snail. In the Netherlands it is a monkey's tail.
peek: English speakers just say at, but much of the world looks at the @ sign and sees an animal or a snack. Italians see a snail, Dutch speakers a little monkey's tail, Russians a dog and Czechs a rolled-up herring.
lede: The @ arrived on almost every keyboard with email, and many languages had no word ready for it. So people named it after what it looked like. The results are a small zoo. Italians call it chiocciola, a snail. The Dutch say apenstaartje, a little monkey's tail. Hebrew speakers call it a shtrudel, after the rolled pastry.

bullets.text: Swedes and Danes call it snabel-a, the a with an elephant's trunk. The curl around the letter looks like a trunk swinging round, and the name is used in everyday speech.
Russian speakers usually call it sobaka, which means dog. Nobody is sure where the name came from; one popular guess is that the shape looks like a dog curled up asleep.

In Czech and Slovak the sign is a zavináč, a rollmop: a fillet of pickled herring rolled around a filling. Greek speakers call it papaki, a duckling, and Finns sometimes call it miukumauku, after a curled-up cat.
Spanish and Portuguese call it arroba, an old unit of weight for goods. A merchant's letter written in 1536 already used @ for a measure of wine, so the sign was a trader's mark long before email.
